      Significant accounting judgements, estimates and assumptions                
      Determination of an onerous contract                                        
      A contract is onerous at initial recognition where the expected fulfilment cash flows, any previously recognised acquisition cash flows, and any cash
      flows arising from the contract, at the date of initial recognition, in total, are a net outflow. The Group uses estimates to determine future expected
      cash flows. The estimation considers available historical information about claims and statistical data relating to events that affect the loss ratio
      such as crime rates, mortality rates, etc. The insurance contracts were determined to be non-onerous on initial recognition.
      Summary of material accounting policies                                     
      FutureMakers Fund                                                           
      This fund is an enterprise and supplier development (ESD) programme. In partnership with Identity FutureFund (Pty) Ltd, the fund was created
      in terms of the Department of Trade and Industry's Code of Good Practice on Black Economic Empowerment 2007, as amended, and
      specifically in terms of the IT charter.                                    
      The Company accounts for this at cost as an investment in a subsidiary. The Group consolidates the fund and holds the investments within the
      fund at fair value. The underlying investments in the fund have been designated as at fair value through profit or loss as this more
      appropriately reflects the basis on which management measures and monitors the performance of the investment. No change was made to
      this designation following the adoption of IFRS 9. In 2018, the partnership agreement was amended to also include BCX. BCX invested an
      amount of R100 million, which is reflected as a financial asset in the BCX stand-alone annual financial statements and included in cash and cash
      equivalents in the Group annual financial statements.                       
      Investment in associate                                                     
      The Number Portability Company (Pty) Ltd was incorporated in response to Regulations of 2005 that required a national centralised database
      of ported numbers for mobile numbers. The investment has been classified as an associate in line with the requirements of the revised IAS 28
      (Investments in Associates and Joint Ventures). The year-end of the associate, 31 December, is different from that of the Company and the
      impact is not material.                                                     
      Investment in insurance first-party cell captive                            
      Telkom has entered into a first-party cell captive arrangement with Guardrisk. The first-party cell is to insure the life of Telkom’s employees
      and their related parties. Telkom pays insurance premiums to Guardrisk periodically. In the event that a life is lost, the claims are paid from the
      cell captive.                                                               
      The first-party cell is not subject to IFRS 17 as it is not an insurance contract as defined in IFRS 17. The Telkom share subscription is accounted
      for as an IFRS 9 financial asset at fair value through profit or loss.      
      Investment in insurance third-party cell captive                            
      Telkom is a cell captive owner for two third-party cell captive arrangements with Mutual and Federal Risk Financing Limited (MFRF) and
      Guardrisk. Both MFRF and Guardrisk are licensed insurance companies. MFRF underwrites the Telkom device insurance and Guardrisk
      underwrites the Telkom life insurance.                                      
      The device insurance allows Telkom's customers to insure their devices against theft, accidental loss, and accidental physical damage.
      The life insurance allows customers to insure lives with the main product being the death benefit cover.
      Both third-party cells are ring-fenced insurance businesses and Telkom’s participation is restricted to the results of the insurance businesses.
      Based on the nature of the shareholder and subscription and intermediary contracts between Telkom and MFRF and Guardrisk, Telkom
      compensates the underwriters for claims arising from the contracts issued to the public when the premiums cannot cover those claims.
      The contract between Telkom and the underwriters is classified as reinsurance contracts issued.
      In the Group, the cell captive arrangements effectively represent investments in a separate class of shares in the cell captive insurer (Guardrisk
      and MFRF). The Group concluded that its cell captive arrangement does not satisfy the criteria to be a deemed separate entity and, accordingly,
      is not subject to consolidation.                                            
      Telkom will derecognise the cell captive asset from its statement of financial position in the event that the contract is cancelled, expired or upon
      liquidation of the insurer.                                                 
      Classification                                                              
      Insurance contracts are contracts under which the Group accepts significant insurance risk from its cell captive underwriters (MFRF and
      Guardrisk) by agreeing to compensate the underwriters if a specified uncertain future event covered by the insurance adversely affects the
      third-party policyholders. The contracts issued by the underwriters to the policyholders meet this definition.
      Contract boundary period                                                    
      The measurement of the insurance contracts only considers cash flows within the boundary. Cash flows are within the boundary of an insurance
      contract if they arise from substantive rights and obligations that exist during the reporting period in which the entity can compel the policyholder
      to pay the premiums or in which the entity has a substantive obligation to provide the policyholder with insurance contract services.
      Measurement                                                                 
      The Group applies the premium allocation approach (PAA) on the device and life insurance contracts as they have a coverage period of one year
      or less. Both the device insurance and life insurance do not meet the definition of insurance contracts with direct participating rights.

      Investment in insurance third-party cell captive continued                  
      Measurement continued                                                       
      The Group manages insurance contracts by product lines, i.e. device insurance and life insurance, within the Consumer operating segment.
      Insurance contracts within a product line represent a portfolio of contracts. Each portfolio is further assessed and grouped into three cohorts,
      namely:                                                                     
      – Contracts that are onerous at initial recognition;                        
      – Contracts that, at initial recognition, have no significant possibility of becoming onerous subsequently; and
      – Remaining group contracts.                                                
      All the insurance contracts were determined to be non-onerous on initial recognition.
      Insurance liability measurement                                             
      The insurance cell recognises the insurance contracts with the policyholders at the earlier of:
      – the beginning of the coverage period;                                     
      – the date when the first payment from a policyholder is due or when the first payment is received, if there is no due date; and
      – the date when the insurance cell becomes onerous.                         
      Liability for remaining coverage                                            
      Using the PAA measurement, the liability for remaining coverage is measured as:
      – Insurance premiums received at initial recognition;                       
      – Less insurance acquisition cash flows incurred at initial recognition.    
      Subsequently:                                                               
      – Opening liability for remaining coverage as per the previous reporting period;
      – Add insurance revenue received;                                           
      – Less insurance revenue recognised;                                        
      – Less acquisition costs paid;                                              
      – Add acquisition cash flows incurred in the period; and                    
      – Add interest attributed to the profit share account/investment income over a period.
      Insurance acquisition cash flows incurred                                   
      Insurance acquisition cash flows incurred consist of cash flows that arise from costs of selling, underwriting, insurance acquisition and other
      insurance business operating expenses.                                      
      Liability for Incurred Claims                                               
      Liability for incurred claims consists of claims incurred but not yet honoured and paid. The Group does not adjust for the time value of money
      as the time between providing the insurance service and the related claim date are not more than a year. The fulfilment cash flows are
      determined on an unbiased basis and reflect the Group’s estimate of the claims liability. The estimate considers all information available
      without undue costs relating to the cash flows arising from substantive rights and obligations that exist during the reporting period.
      Acquisition costs                                                           
      The Group accounting policy choice is to expense insurance acquisition cash flows as and when they are incurred, as the insurance coverage
      period is 12 months or less.                                                
      Insurance risk                                                              
      Insurance risk is the risk that the premiums received to cover the insured events are not sufficient to cover the claims liability.
      Telkom is exposed to the risk that should there be insufficient capital available to honour the claims made by the policyholders in the cell
      captive arrangement, it has to recapitalise the cell captive. Therefore, Telkom has accepted significant insurance risk from the underwriters
      in a controlled manner by investing in the businesses that are liable to compensate the third party in the event that a specified risk occurs.
      Insurance contract risk is unpredictable by nature. To determine the insurance premiums, the underwriters use available historical claims
      information and actuarial science techniques.                               
      The underwriter’s risk is that the actual insurance claims liability exceeds the premiums collected from the policyholders.
      The number of claims at any given boundary period cannot be predicted with certainty and is affected by the following unforeseen events that
      may lead to insufficient capital being available to honour customer claims: 
      – Loss rate risk: Risk that the actual experienced losses/claims are higher than that assumed and cannot be covered by collected insurance
       premiums. For device insurance, this relates to claims arising from loss, accidental physical damage or theft of devices. For life insurance, this
       relates to the loss of the insured life or changes in assumed mortality rates.
      – Business volume risk: Risk that the insurance business may not attract and sell sufficient volumes to cover the fixed costs of running the business.
      – Lapse risk: Risk that customers will terminate their contracts prior to contractual maturity.
      – Crime rate risk: Risk that crime levels increase significantly, resulting in a high frequency of claims due to death, for life insurance, and theft,
       for device insurance.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**A. Capital management (7.1.8, p.94) — definitional traps**
- Net debt is defined **excluding lease liabilities** ("net debt (excluding lease liabilities) to EBITDA"). This is a material definitional choice: IFRS 16 lease liabilities are excluded from the leverage metric. Any forecast of reported leverage must reconcile to this ex-lease basis, and the lease-inclusive figure is **not disclosed here** → verification question.
- EBITDA definition is **inclusive of interest revenue and interest on overdue accounts** — i.e., EBITDA is *grossed up* by non-operating interest income. This inflates the denominator and flatters the ratio. Flag for forecast normalization.
- Arithmetic check (Group): 4,524 + 2,069 − 7,723 − 60 = **−1,190** ✓ ties to stated net debt. Company: 4,524 + 2,069 − 4,937 − 29 = **1,627** ✓ ties. Group swung from net debt R540m (FY25) to **net cash R1,190m** (FY26) — a R1,730m deleveraging. Driver is cash rising? No — cash *fell* from 11,054 to 7,723 (−3,331) while debt fell 9,368+2,249=11,617 → 4,524+2,069=6,593 (−5,024). Net effect −5,024 debt reduction vs −3,331 cash = −1,693, plus restricted cash −37 ≈ −1,730 ✓. **Debt repayment outpaced cash burn** — verify source of repayment (asset sales? FCF?).
- Company EBITDA fell 10,433 → 7,177 (−31%) while Group EBITDA rose 11,014 → 12,480 (+13%). Large divergence — Company (Telkom SA stand-alone) EBITDA collapse needs explanation → verification question.

**B. Investment in subsidiaries (7.2.1, p.94) — footnotes**
- `[^1]` "Return on investment is due to the operations of Trudon being integrated with Telkom in the 2023 financial year." — explains the (253) negative carrying line for Trudon; a **legacy integration artifact**, not a current-year impairment. No forecast impact but confirms Trudon is no longer a discrete operating subsidiary.
- `[^2]` "In the current year, Gyro Group was divisionalised within Telkom." — Gyro Group carrying value fell 5 → 0. **Divisionalisation** (not disposal) means the entity was absorbed into Telkom divisions; the R5m derecognition is a reclassification, not a cash event. Verify no gain/loss booked.
- Openserve: cost 11,296, accumulated impairment (4,655) — **impairment unchanged YoY** (4,655 both years), so no FY26 impairment charge on Openserve at Company level. BCX carried at 6,579 with **no accumulated impairment shown** — verify BCX impairment status (note 5.3 referenced).
- Total investment in subsidiaries 13,465 vs 13,477 (−12) — small net movement; reconcile to component lines (Gyro −5, FutureMakers −8, share-based +1, rounding).

**C. Loans to subsidiaries (7.2.2, p.95) — tenor/pricing (relevant to Q-D9 residual)**
- Loan 1: R4.2bn, 5y6m, 3M JIBAR + 1.65%, quarterly interest, capital in 5 instalments, **next R500m due 31 Mar 2027**.
- Loan 2: R4.8bn, 10y, 3M JIBAR + 1.85%, **bullet repayment** at end.
- RCF: R1.2bn committed over 10y, JIBAR + 1.85%; **R378m utilised at 31 Mar 2026**, inside current portion of R878m.
- ECL: general approach, **0.43%** (FY25: 0.88%) and 40% LGD; provision **decreased R15m** (FY25: R25m decrease). Lower ECL rate = improved credit view of Openserve — but note the rate nearly halved; verify driver (rating upgrade vs model change).
- Arithmetic: 8,767 − 15 = 8,752 ✓ ties. Non-current 7,889 + current 878 = 8,767 ✓.
- BCX facility R1bn / 3y6m / JIBAR + 1.65% — **undrawn** at year-end.

**D. Other investments / cell captives (7.2.3, pp.96–99)**
- Insurance contract assets: Device 945 asset / (827) LIC; Life 32 / (16). **No loss component FY25 or FY26** — all contracts non-onerous. Telkom **has opted not to reinsure** its cell-captive insurance risk → retained risk exposure; monitor claims ratio.
- Device insurance reconciliation arithmetic: opening 740 + 205 (P&L) + 0 (cash) = 945 ✓. LIC: (499) + (88) + (240) = (827) ✓. Life: 25 + 7 = 32 ✓; (15) + (1) = (16) ✓.
- Preference dividends received (240) in device LIC cash flows — large; verify nature (cell captive profit extraction) and recurrence.
- FutureMakers Fund: Group FV 102 (FY25 96); Company cost 54 (FY25 62) after disinvestment (8). BCX R100m investment "included in cash and cash equivalents in the Group AFS" — **classification inconsistency** (financial asset at BCX stand-alone vs cash at Group) → verification question.
- Onerous contract judgement: "insurance contracts were determined to be non-onerous on initial recognition" — forward-looking estimate; flag for sensitivity.

### 3. New Questions to Check in Future Sections

- **Q-K1 [HIGH]** — Net debt is disclosed **excluding lease liabilities**. Locate the lease-inclusive net debt / lease liabilities balance (IFRS 16) and the lease-inclusive Net Debt/EBITDA to reconcile the leverage metric used for covenants. (Check debt note / lease note.)
- **Q-K2 [HIGH]** — EBITDA definition **includes interest revenue and interest on overdue accounts**. Quantify this add-back to normalize EBITDA for forecasting and covenant headroom. (Check EBITDA reconciliation / segment note.)
- **Q-K3 [HIGH]** — Company EBITDA fell 31% (10,433→7,177) while Group EBITDA rose 13%. Identify the driver (dividend/management fee elimination, once-off, subsidiary performance). (Check segment/Company income statement.)
- **Q-K4 [MED]** — Group moved to **net cash R1,190m** from net debt R540m; debt repaid R5,024m vs cash down R3,331m. Confirm source of debt repayment (FCF, asset disposal, refinancing) and whether R4.2bn Openserve loan instalments (R500m due 31 Mar 2027) are intra-group only (no Group cash impact). (Check cash flow statement / borrowings note.)
- **Q-K5 [MED]** — Openserve accumulated impairment static at R4,655m; BCX shows **no accumulated impairment**. Confirm BCX impairment test outcome (note 5.3) and whether any FY26 charge arose. (Check note 5.3.)
- **Q-K6 [MED]** — ECL rate on Openserve loans halved (0.88%→0.43%). Confirm driver (credit rating upgrade vs methodology change) and sustainability. (Check credit risk note.)
- **Q-K7 [MED]** — Preference dividends received R240m within device cell-captive LIC cash flows. Confirm nature, recurrence, and P&L/cash classification. (Check cell captive / dividend note.)
- **Q-K8 [LOW]** — BCX R100m FutureMakers investment classified as **cash at Group but financial asset at BCX stand-alone**. Confirm consolidation elimination and cash definition. (Check cash note / consolidation.)
- **Q-K9 [LOW]** — Gyro Group divisionalisation (carrying 5→0): confirm no gain/loss and treatment of any residual assets/liabilities. (Check business combinations / reorganisation note.)
- **Q-K10 [LOW]** — Cell captives **not reinsured**; confirm claims ratio trend and solvency/liquidity capital injection history. (Check insurance risk note / contingent liabilities.)

      7.3 Other financial assets and liabilities                                  
                                                                                  
      Significant accounting judgements, estimates and assumptions                
                                                                                  
      Cash flow treatment of asset finance transactions                           
      The cash flows from BCX asset finance transactions are accounted for in operating activities within the statement of cash flows. Significant
      judgement was involved in concluding the above, which included the following considerations:
      – BCX has a principal revenue-producing activity of providing financing to customers. The provision of financing to customers provides an
       advantage in the overall customer value proposition, from which further opportunities for revenue generation arise. Financing to customers
       is managed on a back-to back basis with the financier, with full disclosure of the identity of the financier in the customer contracts.
       Financing is managed at a customer level, which is also the level at which performance within the business unit is assessed.
      – Margins on deals are actively managed with a track record of gross profit and EBITDA margins enabled through profitable margins
       between the lending rate to the customer and the rate from the financier (over and above the typical equipment outright sale deals).
       Where BCX assumes the credit risk on deals (deals with recourse), the credit risk is managed in line with the Company's credit risk policies
       and practices.                                                             
      Summary of material accounting policies                                     
      Investment in equity fund                                                   
      In 2016, the private sector formed the SA SME Fund, the purpose of which is to stimulate investments in high-potential small and medium
      enterprises (SMEs). This partnership between the fund and the accredited companies will also build a high-quality mentorship cohort to support
      said enterprises and entrepreneurs. Pursuant to this initiative, various leading private sector entities committed to providing equity funding to the
      fund.                                                                       
      In the 2022 financial year, Telkom entered into an agreement with this fund in terms of which Telkom will provide equity funding through share
      subscriptions to the value of R10 million. Telkom does not have control over the fund as it only holds 0.72% interest in the fund. The investment
      is classified at fair value through profit or loss. The fair value of the investment is equivalent to its cost price.
      Asset finance payables                                                      
      The Group leases equipment to certain customers. These leases are accounted for as either operating leases or finance leases. In certain cases,
      BCX finances the purchase of the underlying equipment through securitisation of the underlying rental schedules. Where the derecognition
      criteria for the sale of the lease receivable to the financial institution in terms of IFRS 9 has been met, the lease receivable is derecognised. If the
      derecognition criteria are not met and the Group does not transfer all risks and rewards (i.e. credit risk), the lease receivable is not derecognised.
      The Group accounts for the liability related to the inflow from the financial institutions for the financing of these leases as asset finance payables.
      BCX supplier finance arrangements with extended payment terms               
      BCX participates in SFAs with extended payment terms and the trade payables subject to this arrangement are classified as other financial
      liabilities. The assessment of SFAs, and whether they result in changes to the trade payables classification to interest-bearing debt, takes into
      consideration numerous factors, which include the impact of the arrangement on the supplier’s payment term, the nature of the relationships
      between the Group and the funders, changes in cash flows, whether there are any guarantees provided by the Group to the funders, as well as
      whether the supplier has discharged the Group from its obligation.          
      Considering the above assessment at the reporting date, the Group had invoices subject to the SFAs that met the requirements to be reclassified
      as other financial liabilities.                                             
      R61 million (31 March 2025: R94 million) of the total other financial liabilities is subject to supplier financing arrangements with extended
      payment terms. Refer to note 7.1.5 for liquidity risk disclosure.

      7.3 Other financial assets and liabilities continued                        
      SMME loans                                                                  
      The Group grants interest-free loans for Broad-Based Black Economic Empowerment (B-BBEE) scorecard purposes. Based on the Group’s
      business model of managing the interest-free loans for small, medium and micro enterprises (SMMEs), subsequently interest-free loans are
      measured at amortised cost as they are held with the objective to collect contractual cash flows that are solely payments of the principal amount
      outstanding and/or interest on the outstanding amount.                      
      As required by IFRS 9, interest-free loans are initially recognised at fair value plus transaction costs that are directly attributable to the
      acquisition or issue. The SMME loans are not granted at fair value as they are interest-free.
      On initial recognition, the difference between the fair value and the transaction price (loan amount) is recognised as a loss in the statement
      of profit or loss and other comprehensive income. Although the loans are granted for B-BBEE purposes, due to points being earned through
      financing the SMMEs, the loss is recognised as a finance cost.              
      Telkom has appointed Absa Group Ltd to act as its agent for the purposes of managing and administering the ESD funding loans. The loan
      amounts for the seven borrowers range from a minimum of R2.5 million to a maximum of R10 million. The loans are all at a zero-interest rate
      and have different instalments and period terms.                            
      Aligned with IFRS 9 principles, the Group uses the general approach in calculating expected credit losses on loans. The SMMEs' credit risk scores
      are not publicly available and there is currently no history available in which the credit risk can be assessed. Based on the nature and size of the
      SMMEs, their credit risk is regarded as significant, thus a lifetime expected credit loss will be calculated. In the current and prior financial years,
      no expected credit losses were recognised on the SMME loans.                
      Derivatives                                                                 
      Derivatives held for risk management purposes include hedges that either meet the hedge accounting requirements or economic hedges that do
      not meet the hedge accounting requirements. Derivatives are carried as financial assets when the fair value is positive and as financial liabilities
      when the fair value is negative.                                            
      Derivatives that do not meet the hedge accounting requirements              
      The Group uses forward exchange contracts and interest rate swaps to economically hedge its foreign exchange and interest rate exposures.
      This relates to the "Other" category of forward exchange contracts as referred to in note 7.1.6. These derivative instruments are measured at fair
      value through profit or loss.                                               
      Derivatives that meet the hedge accounting requirements                     
      The Group uses forward exchange contracts to hedge its exposure to changes attributable to movements in the spot exchange rate of its firm
      commitments. These derivatives are designated as fair value hedges.         
      Fair value hedges                                                           
      The foreign forward exchange contracts, designated as fair value hedges, are being used to hedge the exposure to changes attributable to
      movements in the spot exchange rates of firm commitments.                   
      The Group implements fair value hedge accounting where the hedging relationship meets the requirements of IAS 39.
      Hedge effectiveness is determined at inception of the hedge relationship and at each reporting period-end through an assessment of the
      hedged items and hedging instruments to determine whether there is still an economic relationship between the two. Hedge ineffectiveness
      arises from the impact of the counterparty’s assessment of the Group’s credit risk on the fair value of the forward exchange contracts, which
      is not reflected in the fair value of the hedged item, and the difference in the timing of the maturity of the derivatives, and the settlement of the
      hedged item.

### [ANALYST QUERY / EMPHASIS]
Scrutinize key accounting policies, unusual movements, and forward guidance.

### [SECTION READING RESPONSE / DETERMINATION]
### 1. Answers to Stored Questions for This Section

**Q-D1 / GG1 / HH1 / AAA1 / CCC1 / CCC2 [HIGH] — residual: cash flow hedge reserve & settlement cash-flow classification.**
**Partially answered.** §7.3 (pp.100–103) confirms the Group operates **fair value hedges** (FX forwards on firm commitments) and **economic hedges not qualifying for hedge accounting** (FX forwards and interest rate swaps, FVTPL). This is material to the residual question:
- Fair value hedges: changes in fair value of the hedging instrument go to **P&L** (with offsetting fair value adjustment to the hedged firm commitment), *not* to a cash flow hedge reserve. The "Changes in fair value used for calculating hedge ineffectiveness" of **R378m (FY2026)** and **R164m (FY2025)** (Group) are P&L-affecting, not OCI.
- Economic hedges (FVTPL): all fair value movements hit P&L directly.
- **Implication:** the earlier concern about a *cash flow hedge reserve* being recycled through OCI appears **not applicable to these instruments** — there is no cash flow hedge reserve movement from these FX/IRS derivatives. The residual question now narrows to: (i) whether any *separate* cash flow hedge relationships exist elsewhere (e.g., interest rate hedges on debt designated as cash flow hedges) — **not evidenced here**; and (ii) the **cash-flow statement classification of derivative settlements** (operating vs financing/investing) — **not disclosed in §7.3**. Carry forward as narrowed residual (see Q-J1/Q-J2 below).

**Q-D9 / GG4 / HH4 / II4 / AAA16 [MED] — residual: per-contract tenor & repatriation purpose.**
**Not addressed.** §7.3 covers SMME loans, equity fund, cell captive, asset finance payables, SFAs and derivatives — no FX/repatriation or per-contract tenor disclosure. **Remains open.**

**Q-K1–Q-K10 (from §7.2):** None of these relate to §7.3 evidence (they concern subsidiary/Openserve loan matters). **All remain open** and are carried forward.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**No footnote markers (`[^1]`, `*`) appear in the supplied §7.3 evidence.** No missing-footnote verification question is therefore triggered for this section. However, several **small-print accounting judgements and policy qualifications** carry forecast-relevant implications:

**(a) Cash flow treatment of BCX asset finance transactions (p.100) — operating classification.**
- Management asserts BCX's principal revenue-producing activity is **providing financing to customers**, managed **back-to-back with the financier**, with margins actively managed. Consequence: asset finance cash flows are classified in **operating activities**, not investing/financing.
- **Forecast implication:** BCX asset finance inflows/outflows inflate *operating* cash flow and are **not** captured in capex or financing lines. This distorts FCFE and cash conversion metrics — a verification question is raised (Q-L1).
- **Credit risk qualification:** "Where BCX assumes the credit risk on deals (deals with recourse)" — implies a **recourse vs non-recourse split** exists but is **not quantified**. Verification question raised (Q-L2).

**(b) Asset finance payables — IFRS 9 derecognition judgement (p.100).**
- Where derecognition criteria for sale of lease receivable to the financial institution are **met**, receivable is derecognised; where **not met** (credit risk not transferred), receivable stays on balance sheet and the financing inflow is recorded as an **asset finance payable**.
- **Forecast implication:** the **R130m non-current + R172m current = R302m** asset finance payables (FY2026) represent **on-balance-sheet financing of lease receivables** — effectively debt-like. This must be considered in net debt / leverage analysis (Q-L3). Note the movement: non-current fell R205m→R130m; current rose R155m→R172m — a **reclassification/amortisation pattern** worth verifying (Q-L4).

**(c) BCX supplier finance arrangements (SFAs) — reclassification to other financial liabilities (p.100).**
- **R61m (FY2025: R94m)** of other financial liabilities is SFA-related, reclassified from trade payables to **interest-bearing debt-like** other financial liabilities. The assessment considered payment-term extension, funder relationships, guarantees, and supplier discharge.
- **Forecast implication:** SFA balance is **declining (R94m→R61m)** — a working-capital/leverage tailwind but also a signal of **reduced supplier financing reliance**. Must be added to debt-like items for covenant/leverage purposes (Q-L5). Cross-reference to note 7.1.5 liquidity risk (Q-L6).

**(d) SMME loans — interest-free, IFRS 9 fair-value loss to finance cost (p.102).**
- Interest-free B-BBEE loans (7 borrowers, R2.5m–R10m each) measured at amortised cost; **initial fair-value vs transaction-price difference recognised as a loss in P&L, classified as a finance cost** (because B-BBEE points are earned).
- **No expected credit losses recognised** in current or prior year despite management stating SMME credit risk is "significant" and "no history available."
- **Forecast implication:** (i) a recurring **finance cost drag** from new SMME loan originations (Q-L7); (ii) **zero ECL** on "significant" credit risk is an aggressive assumption — potential future impairment (Q-L8). Balances: non-current R46m (FY2025 R77m), current R36m (FY2025 nil) — total R82m vs R77m prior; the **current/non-current reclassification** (R77m non-current → R46m + R36m current) implies amortisation/repayment schedule (Q-L9).

**(e) Investment in equity fund (SA SME Fund) — 0.72%, FVTPL, fair value = cost (p.100).**
- R10m carried at cost = fair value; **no control** (0.72%). No fair-value remeasurement. Low forecast relevance but a **stale-valuation flag** (Q-L10).

**(f) Derivatives — fair value hedge accounting under IAS 39 (p.102–103).**
- Fair value hedges of FX on firm commitments; hedge ineffectiveness from counterparty credit risk and maturity timing mismatch; **ineffective portion immaterial** in both years.
- **Nominal amounts:** Group FX forwards R4,488m (FY2025 R3,859m); Company R3,149m (FY2025 R3,379m). **Carrying amounts:** Group assets R105m / liabilities R(140)m (FY2026) vs R35m / R(61)m (FY2025); Company R90m / R(99)m vs R22m / R(50)m.
- **Forecast implication:** the **gross-up of derivative assets and liabilities** (both sides large) reflects **firm commitment hedging of imported equipment/spectrum** — a leading indicator of **capex/opex FX exposure** (Q-L11). The **R378m FY2026 vs R164m FY2025** change in fair value used for ineffectiveness is a **P&L volatility driver** to model (Q-L12).

**(g) Arithmetic / reconciliation checks on §7.3 table (p.101):**
- **Other financial assets — non-current:** 63 = 46 (SMME) + 17 (FVTPL: 10 equity fund + 7 cell captive). ✔ Ties.
- **Other financial assets — current:** 196 = 36 (SMME current) + 160 (derivatives: 105 FEC + 53 firm commitments + 2 IRS). ✔ Ties.
- **Other financial liabilities — non-current:** (130) = asset finance payables (130). ✔
- **Other financial liabilities — current:** (419) = (233) amortised cost [(172) asset finance + (61) SFA] + (186) derivatives [(140) FEC + (23) firm commitments + (23) IRS]. ✔ Ties.
- **Derivative asset/liability cross-check to p.103:** Group FEC assets 105 / liabilities (140) — **matches** p.101 FEC lines. ✔ Company 90/(99) matches. ✔
- **No arithmetic tension identified** in the §7.3 table. However, the **fair value hedge carrying amounts on p.103 (assets 105 / liabilities 140)** are stated as the *hedging instrument* carrying amounts; the p.101 derivative lines include **both hedge-accounted and economic (FVTPL) derivatives** — the split between hedge-accounted vs economic is **not separately reconciled** (Q-L13).

- **Q-L7 [MED]:** Quantify the **finance cost** arising from SMME loan initial fair-value losses in FY2026 and expected FY2027 originations — check finance costs note.
- **Q-L8 [MED]:** Justify **zero ECL** on SMME loans despite "significant" credit risk and no history — check ECL/credit risk note and subsequent events.
- **Q-L9 [LOW]:** Confirm **SMME loan repayment schedule** driving current/non-current split (R46m non-current / R36m current) — check liquidity/maturity note.
- **Q-L10 [LOW]:** Confirm **SA SME Fund** fair value still equals cost (R10m) and any impairment indicators — check fair value hierarchy note (7.1.6/7.1.7).
- **Q-L11 [HIGH]:** Identify the **underlying hedged items** (imported equipment, spectrum, opex) behind the **R4,488m nominal FX forwards** and link to capex/spectrum commitments — check capital commitments and spectrum notes.
- **Q-L12 [MED]:** Model the **P&L fair value movement (R378m FY2026 vs R164m FY2025)** and confirm whether any portion is deferred/recognised in OCI — check OCI statement and hedge reserve note.
- **Q-L13 [MED]:** Reconcile **hedge-accounted vs economic (FVTPL) derivative split** — p.101 derivative lines vs p.103 hedge-accounted carrying amounts — check note 7.1.6.
- **Q-L14 [HIGH]:** Confirm whether **any cash flow hedge relationships** (e.g., interest rate hedges on debt) exist outside the fair value hedges disclosed here — check debt/hedging note and OCI.
- **Q-L15 [MED]:** Confirm **cash-flow statement classification of derivative settlements** (operating vs investing/financing) — check Statement of Cash Flows.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**Footnote [^1] — Group tax expense +R350m to R1,208m "primarily due to increase in taxable profits."**
- Verification tension: Group PBT must have risen materially, but the *effective rate* rose only from 19.1% → 25.4% (+6.3pp). The +R350m absolute increase is consistent with both higher PBT and a higher effective rate. **Need PBT (Note 9/income statement) to reconcile: Tax ÷ PBT should equal 25.4%.** Flag as arithmetic check (Q-T1).
- The footnote attributes the increase to "taxable profits" but footnote [^6] attributes the *rate* increase to prior-year property disposals (80% capital gain inclusion). These are two different drivers — the [^1] narrative is incomplete/misleading. **Verification question: what is the split of the R350m increase between volume (PBT) and rate (mix) effects?**

**Footnote [^2] — "Provisions and other allowances" movement "mainly due to IFRS 16 lease liabilities… remeasurements and additions."**
- This is a **critical telecom-specific disclosure**: deferred tax on IFRS 16 lease liabilities (and corresponding ROU assets) is driving the deferred tax line. The +R106m credit (vs +R674m prior year) implies **lease remeasurement/additions decelerated sharply YoY**. 
- Implication for forecast: deferred tax on leases is a **non-cash timing item** tied to tower/network lease portfolio growth. If tower MLA additions slow, this deferred tax credit shrinks → **cash tax rate converges toward effective rate**. Flag: need Note 8.2 (deferred tax) to quantify the IFRS 16 deferred tax balance and confirm the ROU/lease liability deferred tax gross-up (Q-T2).
- Also note: the prior-year R674m credit was unusually large — suggests a **one-off lease remeasurement** in FY2025 (possibly tower MLA renewal or discount-rate reset). **Verification: was FY2025 inflated by a non-recurring lease remeasurement?**

**Footnote [^3] — "Non-deductible write-offs in respect of the previous acquisition of BCX" (R23m deferred tax).**
- Small but persistent (R9m prior year). Confirms **BCX legacy tax friction** continues. Immaterial to forecast but flag as recurring ~R10–25m non-deductible drag (Q-T3).

**Footnote [^4] — Overprovision for prior year "mainly due to capital allowances on fixed assets recognised in prior years."**
- R10m deferred overprovision (vs R69m prior year) and R9m current overprovision (vs R2m underprovision prior year). The **sharp decline in prior-year overprovision (R69m → R10m)** suggests the capital-allowance catch-up benefit is **exhausting**. Forecast implication: **do not extrapolate prior-year tax credits**; assume clean current-year rate going forward (Q-T4).

**Footnote [^5] — Profit on sale of assets: rate benefit fell from (5.8)% to (0.9)% Group.**
- Driven by **reduced Gyro Properties disposals** vs prior year. Company: prior year included **Swiftnet sale** (80% capital gain inclusion). 
- Forecast implication: **FY2026 has minimal property-disposal tax shield**; FY2025 was inflated. **Normalised effective rate is closer to 25–26% than the 19.1% FY2025 print.** This is the single most important tax forecast input (Q-T5).

**Footnote [^6] — Effective rate +6.3pp to 25.4% Group; Company 5.8% → 19.9%.**
- Group 25.4% is now **close to the 27% statutory rate** — limited remaining shields. Company 19.9% still below statutory due to **insurance cell captive exempt income, capital losses, IFRS 2 adjustment**.
- **Forecast anchor: use ~25–26% Group effective rate for FY2027**, not the 19.1% FY2025 base. Company rate is volatile (5.8% → 19.9%) — do not use Company rate for Group forecasting.

**Arithmetic checks performed:**
- Current tax (273) + prior year 9 + deferred (944) = (1,208) ✓ ties to Taxation line.
- SA normal company taxation (264) = current (273) + prior 9 ✓.
- Deferred components: (758) + 106 + (325) + 23 + 10 = (944) ✓ ties.
- Reconciliation: 27.0 − 1.6 = 25.4 ✓ ties to effective rate.
- **Discrepancy flag:** "Decreased by adjustments" subtotal (1.6)% but individual lines sum to: (1.6)+(1.1)+(1.4)+(0.5)+(0.1)+(0.1)+(0.9)+(0.2)+(0.2) = **+2.5% net of negatives** — the (1.6) subtotal appears to net only the *decreases* and excludes the *increases* (non-deductible, capex, interest). **Verification question Q-T6: confirm the reconciliation subtotal convention (decreases-only vs net).**

- **Deferred tax credit normalising:** FY2025 R674m "provisions/other" credit likely contained non-recurring lease remeasurement; FY2026 R106m is the more normalised run-rate → **cash tax rate converging toward effective rate**.
- **Cash tax rate** to be confirmed from cash flow statement (Q-T7) — deferred tax R944m is non-cash, so cash tax ≈ current tax R273m less prior-year adjustments.
- **Assessed losses:** R325m utilised in FY2026 (rising from R236m) — need carried-forward balance (Q-T8) to model remaining shield.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**Footnote [^1] — "Group tax expense increased by R350m to R1 208m… primarily due to the increase in the Group's taxable profits."**
- Arithmetic check: R1 208m − R858m = R350m. ✓ Consistent.
- But the *composition* contradicts the narrative. The R350m increase is driven almost entirely by **deferred tax** (R944m vs R376m = +R568m), not current tax (R273m vs R280m = −R7m). Current tax actually *fell*. The "increase in taxable profits" claim is therefore a loose characterisation — the real driver is the swing in deferred tax lines: capital allowances deferred tax fell (R758m vs R892m = −R134m benefit) while provisions/allowances deferred tax flipped from a R674m credit to a R106m credit (−R568m swing) and tax-loss deferred tax worsened (R325m vs R236m = −R89m). **Verification question raised (Q-T1).**

**Footnote [^2] — "movement in provisions and allowances is mainly due to the IFRS 16 lease liabilities that increased as a result of remeasurements and additions."**
- This is the single largest swing in the tax note: the provisions/allowances deferred tax credit collapsed from R674m to R106m (−R568m). Attributing this to IFRS 16 lease liability remeasurements/additions means the **lease liability balance grew materially in FY2026**, generating a larger deductible temporary difference that is *recognised more slowly* (or the prior-year credit was a catch-up). This is a direct read-across to the lease liability / tower MLA disclosure elsewhere. **Verification question raised (Q-T2).**
- Implication for forecast: deferred tax on leases is non-cash and volatile; it should be modelled separately from the cash tax rate. The 25.4% effective rate is *not* a proxy for cash tax.

**Footnote [^3] — BCX non-deductible write-offs (R23m deferred tax, vs R9m prior).**
- Persistent, small, recurring non-deductible BCX write-off drag. Immaterial to forecast but confirms BCX integration write-offs still flowing through tax. **Verification question raised (Q-T3).**

**Footnote [^4] — "decrease in overprovision/underprovision is mainly due to capital allowances on fixed assets recognised in prior years."**
- Prior-year overprovision deferred tax fell from R69m to R10m. This is a **one-off normalisation tailwind exhausting** — the prior-year capital-allowance overprovision shield is largely spent. Supports a structurally higher effective rate going forward. **Verification question raised (Q-T4).**

**Footnote [^5] — property disposals (Gyro Properties) and Swiftnet sale (Company).**
- Group: profit-on-sale tax benefit fell from −5.8% to −0.9% of the rate — the **prior-year property disposal shield is exhausted**. Company: Swiftnet sale (80% capital gain inclusion) drove the prior-year −18.0%; now −0.5%. Confirms the FY2025 effective rate (19.1% Group / 5.8% Company) was flattered by one-offs and is **not a sustainable base**. **Verification question raised (Q-T5).**

**Footnote [^6] — effective rate bridge.**
- Group 25.4% vs 27.0% statutory = −1.6% net. Company 19.9% vs 27.0% = −7.1% net, driven by non-taxable income (−6.9%) and dividends received (−5.4%). The Company rate is structurally low due to **intercompany dividend exemption** — relevant to holding-company cash repatriation and dividend capacity. **Verification question raised (Q-T6).**
- Arithmetic check on Group bridge: 27.0 − 1.6 (non-taxable) + 1.1 (non-deductible) + 1.4 (capex) − 0.5 (IFRS 2) + 0.1 (interest/penalties) + 0.1 (other disallowed) − 0.9 (prior yr) − 0.2 (other taxes) − 0.2 (discontinued) = 26.3%, not 25.4%. **Reconciliation discrepancy of ~0.9pp — flag (Q-T7).** (Note: the "Decreased by the following adjustments: (1.6)" subtotal appears to net only the non-taxable block; the individual add-backs below it are not cleanly additive to the printed 25.4%. Needs the full bridge to reconcile.)

**Discontinued operation tax (R199m prior year, nil current).**
- FY2025 included R199m tax on the discontinued operation (Swiftnet). FY2026 continuing-operations tax of R1 208m is the clean base. **Verification question raised (Q-T8).**

**Judgement/uncertainty language (top of note).**
- "Tax assets are only recognised when amounts receivable are certain"; "substantial differences between the taxation charge… and current tax payments." This is boilerplate but flags **unrecognised deferred tax assets** (likely tax losses in loss-making subsidiaries / foreign ops) that could reverse. **Verification question raised (Q-T9).**

---

### 3. New Questions to Check in Future Sections

- **Q-T2** [HIGH] — Quantify IFRS 16 lease liability remeasurements/additions in FY2026 driving the R568m provisions/allowances deferred tax swing. Cross-check to lease note (IFRS 16 maturity/liability table) and tower MLA disclosure.
- **Q-T3** [LOW] — Confirm BCX non-deductible write-offs (R23m) are recurring or tapering; check BCX/impairment notes.

- **Q-T6** [MED] — Company effective rate 19.9% driven by intercompany dividend exemption; check dividend/cash repatriation note and holding-company liquidity for dividend capacity.
- **Q-T7** [HIGH] — **Arithmetic discrepancy**: Group effective-rate bridge sums to ~26.3% vs printed 25.4% (~0.9pp gap). Obtain full additive bridge or confirm which lines are memo-only. Check §8.2 and any tax reconciliation annexure.
- **Q-T8** [LOW] — Confirm discontinued-operation tax (R199m FY2025) is fully non-recurring; check discontinued operations note.
- **Q-T9** [MED] — Identify unrecognised deferred tax assets (tax losses in foreign/loss-making ops) and expiry; check §8.2 and segment/foreign ops notes.
- **Q-T9a** [MED] — Cash tax paid vs tax expense: given "substantial differences" language, obtain cash tax paid from cash flow statement to derive cash tax rate for FCFE.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**Footnote [^1] — DTA recoverability judgement (the critical forward-looking claim):**
- Management asserts: (i) tax losses "will not continue" and "no additional tax losses will arise within the foreseeable future"; (ii) the FY2023 impairment-driven DTA "will continue to be utilised within approximately five years through the use of the assets"; (iii) utilisation is "evident in the reduction of the DTA attributable to the movement in capital allowances."
- **Arithmetic tension to flag:** The capital allowances *movement* in P&L is **negative R759m** (Group), i.e. a *reduction* of the DTA — consistent with utilisation. But the *closing capital allowances balance* moved from **R(2,305)m to R(3,057)m**, a **R752m increase in the net deferred tax liability**. Footnote [^3] attributes this to "higher acquisitions in the current year" increasing the accounting base of PPE/intangible assets. So the same line is simultaneously (a) being utilised (P&L credit direction) and (b) growing as a liability from capex. These are not contradictory but the net presentation obscures the gross utilisation — **verification question raised** (Q-T11).
- The "five-year business plan" and "approximately five years" utilisation window is a **hard forecast dependency**: if capex (and hence capital allowance generation) slows, or if the five-year plan profitability assumption weakens, the DTA is at risk of impairment. This is a direct input to the effective tax rate forecast.

**Footnote [^2] — IFRS 16 lease liabilities:**
- Confirms lease remeasurements/additions flow through deferred tax as a *provisions and other allowances* item. For forecasting: lease liability additions create a deductible temporary difference (DTA increase) that is **non-cash**; do not model it as cash tax. The closing provisions/allowances DTA of **R4,868m** is now the single largest positive component of the net DTA and is materially lease-linked — a key sensitivity if tower MLA (master lease agreement) renewals or indexation change.

**Footnote [^3] — capital allowances / capex link:**
- Explicitly ties the growing capital-allowance deferred tax *liability* to "higher acquisitions in the current year" (PPE + intangibles). This is the deferred-tax shadow of the capex line — **cross-check against the cash flow statement capex and the capex-to-revenue ratio** (Q-T12).

**Footnote [^4] — tax losses:**
- Group tax-loss DTA fell **R1,675m → R1,339m (−R336m)**; Company **R1,302m → R776m (−R526m)**. Footnote says "mainly due to utilisation of tax losses accumulated in prior years." This is the clearest evidence that the assessed-loss shield is being consumed — consistent with the §8.1 finding that the effective rate is normalising toward the statutory rate. **Forecast implication:** the low effective-tax-rate benefit from assessed losses is a *depleting* asset; do not extrapolate the FY2026 19.1% rate.

**Reconciliation check (arithmetic):**
- Opening 3,637 + P&L/opening movements (967) + OCI 8 = **2,678**, vs stated closing **2,701** → **R23m unexplained gap**. The "Common control transactions/business combinations" line (+R23m) appears to be the reconciling item but is presented *within* the movement block, creating a double-count risk. **Flag as verification question** (Q-T13).
- Components sum: (3,057) + 4,868 + 0 + (1) + 1,339 + (448) = **2,701** ✓ (components tie).
- DTA assets 2,703 + liabilities (2) = **2,701** ✓.

**Missing footnote text:** No footnote markers in this section lack a definition — all four ([^1]–[^4]) are present. No missing-footnote question required here.

### 2. Forensic Verification of This Section (Tax Cash Reconciliation)

**A. Reconciliation arithmetic check (Group):**

| Line | FY26 (Rm) | FY25 (Rm) |
|---|---|---|
| Cash tax paid (opening) | (32) | (396) |
| Opening net tax receivable/(payable) | 32 | (396) → wait, opening = 32? |
| Current tax charge | (32) | (396) |
| Discontinued ops | — | — |
| Closing net tax receivable/(payable) | (32) | 32 |

**Verification flag — arithmetic tension:** The table as captured shows *opening* net tax position of **R32m receivable** (FY26) and **R(396)m payable** (FY25), with *closing* of **R(32)m payable** (FY26) and **R32m receivable** (FY25). The roll-forward (opening + current tax + interest + discontinued = closing) does **not** visibly tie for either year from the captured figures. This is a **capture/formatting ambiguity** (column misalignment in the extracted table), not necessarily a report error — but it must be verified against the printed PDF. → **Q-T17**.

**B. Cash tax paid collapse — the single most important forecast signal:**
- Group cash tax paid fell from **R396m (FY25) → R32m (FY26)**, a **−92%** decline.
- Current tax *charge* also fell **R610m → R265m** (−57%).
- **Forensic implication:** A collapse in cash tax paid alongside a still-substantial current tax charge is consistent with (i) large **assessed-loss / capital-allowance utilisation** (the DTA depletion flagged in §8.2), (ii) **discontinued-operation tax credits** (FY25 shows R75m credit), or (iii) **withholding/interest tax timing**. For forecasting, **do not extrapolate FY26's R32m as a run-rate** — it is almost certainly a trough year driven by loss utilisation. → **Q-T18** (confirm driver of the collapse).

**C. Company vs Group divergence:**
- Company cash tax paid **R147m (FY26) vs R66m (FY25)** — *increased* 123%, opposite direction to Group.
- Company current tax charge **R123m vs R86m** — increased.
- **Forensic implication:** The Group's tax collapse is driven at **subsidiary/opco level** (loss utilisation, likely OpCo/BCX/Gyro or discontinued Swiftnet), while the **HoldCo** is paying *more* tax. This matters for **dividend upstreaming capacity** and **HoldCo cash flow forecasting** — the HoldCo is a net tax payer even as Group tax falls. → **Q-T19**.

**D. Footnote [^1] (share scheme shares):** Only footnote in section; relates to 6,164,800 no-consideration shares under the employee share scheme. **No tax/lease/spectrum commentary** — benign for forecasting, but confirms **no share buyback/cancellation in FY26** (shares in issue flat at 511,140,239). Relevant to **EPS denominator stability** and **dividend per share** forecasting.

      9.3 Non-distributable reserves                                              
      Summary of material accounting policies                                     
      Non-distributable reserves                                                  
      Non-distributable reserves include reserves that have been grouped together as accounting reserves, which have arisen as a result of the
      specific requirements in the accounting standards.                          
      Non-distributable reserves include the following:                           
      – Translation reserve: This reserve comprises foreign currency translation differences arising from the translation of annual financial
       statements of the Group’s foreign entities into South African rand.        
      – Treasury shares: This reserve represents the treasury shares as well as the amounts paid by Telkom to its subsidiary, Rossal No 65 (Pty) Ltd,
       for the acquisition of Telkom's shares to be utilised in terms of the Telkom Group employee share scheme.
      – Shares repurchased for the purpose of the Telkom Group employee share scheme.
      Treasury shares                                                             
      Where the Group acquires shares for the Telkom Group employee share scheme, these shares are measured at acquisition cost and disclosed
      as a reduction of equity. No gain or loss is recognised in profit or loss on the purchase, sale, issue or cancellation of the Group's own equity
      instruments. Such shares are not remeasured for changes in fair value. Any difference between the historical par value of the shares acquired
      and the consideration transferred for the acquisition of the shares is accounted for as an adjustment to retained earnings.
      Where the Group chooses or is required to buy equity instruments from another party to satisfy its obligations to its employees under the
      share-based payment arrangement by delivery of its own shares, the transaction is accounted for as equity-settled. This applies regardless of
      whether the employees’ rights to the equity instruments were granted by the Group itself, or by its shareholders, or were settled by either the
      Group or its shareholders.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**Footnote `[^1]` (Openserve share-based compensation reserve) — unpacked:**
- Openserve became 100% owned from **1 September 2022** (carve-out date).
- For shares granted **before** 1 Sep 2022 where Openserve has **no obligation to pay**, Telkom Company bears the settlement obligation → equity-settled **in Telkom Company only** (not Group).
- Post-carve-out services rendered by Openserve employees → reserve increased in **current year by R1m (FY25: R9m)** with **corresponding entry to investment in Openserve** (i.e., capitalised into the investment carrying value, not P&L).
- **Implication:** This is a **Company-only, non-cash, declining** adjustment. The sharp fall from R9m → R1m signals the pre-carve-out grant pool is nearly fully vested/expired. Forecast impact: negligible going forward; do **not** model as recurring opex.
- **Verification tension:** The footnote says "increased in the current financial year by R1 million" but the table shows the Openserve line as **+1 (FY26) and +9 (FY25)** — consistent. However, the **Company column total still does not foot** (see Q-EQ10). The footnote does not explain the residual.

**Treasury shares policy (small print):**
- Measured at **acquisition cost**, disclosed as **reduction of equity**; **no FV remeasurement**; no gain/loss on purchase/sale/issue/cancellation.
- Difference between **par value** and consideration → **retained earnings adjustment**.
- **Forecast implication:** Treasury share movements are **equity-neutral to P&L**; only affect equity reserves and EPS denominator (share count). Flag for EPS/share-count modelling, not earnings.

**Translation reserve (policy only, no numbers):**
- Comprises FX translation differences on foreign entities into ZAR. **No quantum disclosed in this section** → cannot size FX translation impact on equity/OCI from §9.3 alone. Ties to Q-EQ13 (repatriation) and Q-T24.

**Missing footnote check:** No orphan footnote markers detected in the supplied §9.3 text beyond `[^1]`, which is defined. **No missing-footnote flag required for this section.**

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**No footnote markers (`[^1]`, `*`, note refs) are present in the supplied §9.4 evidence.** The only small-print qualifications are the two bolded narrative lines in §9.3 (carried into this capture):

1. **"The reserve also represents amounts paid by Telkom to its subsidiary, Rossal No 65 (Pty) Ltd, for the acquisition of Telkom's shares to be utilised in terms of the Telkom Group employee share scheme."**
   - Implication: the non-distributable reserve is a **funding vehicle for the employee share scheme**, not a distributable earnings reserve. It is **non-cash** at Group level (intra-group) but **cash-consuming at Company level** (Telkom pays Rossal to buy Telkom shares).
   - Forecast impact: any increase in scheme funding reduces Company cash but is eliminated on Group consolidation. Watch for **scheme top-up** in FY2027 that would depress Company FCFE without affecting Group FCFE.

2. **"All shares will be allocated to employees as part of the Telkom Group employee share scheme."**
   - Implication: the **17,100,451 treasury shares (R1,005m fair value)** are earmarked for employee allocation — they are **not** available for cancellation or resale to third parties. This caps the potential share-count reduction and means the **diluted share count** should include these shares as eventual employee allocations.
   - Forecast impact: use **17.1m shares** as the scheme overhang; do not model them as buyback-accretive.

This is consistent with **intra-group dividend elimination** (Company declares to Group; Group eliminates the portion paid to itself). However, the R23m gap is **not explained** in the evidence — **new verification question Q-DIV1**.

This is a **major forecast input**: dividend payout ratio, FCFE coverage, and net debt trajectory all shift. **Q-DIV4**: confirm dividend per share (DPS) and payout ratio — not disclosed in this section.

      10. Employee benefits                                                       
                                                                                  
      10.1 Employee benefits summary                                              
                                                                                  
      Significant judgements, estimates and assumptions                           
      The Group provides defined benefit plans for certain post-employment benefits. The obligation and assets related to each of the post-
      retirement benefits are determined through an actuarial valuation. The actuarial valuation relies heavily on assumptions as disclosed in
      note 10.1. The assumptions determined by management make use of information obtained from the Group's employment agreements with
      staff and pensioners, market-related returns on similar investments, market-related discount rates and other available information. The
      assumptions concerning the interest on assets and expected change in liabilities are determined on a uniform basis, considering long-term
      historical returns and future estimates of returns and medical inflation expectations. In the event that further changes in assumptions are
      required, the future amounts of post-employment benefits may be affected materially.
      The discount rate reflects the average timing of the estimated defined benefit payments. The discount rate is based on long-term South
      African Government bonds with the longest maturity period as reported by the JSE debt market. The discount rate is expected to follow the
      trend of inflation.                                                         
      The interest cost on the defined benefit obligation and the interest on assets are accounted for through the net interest cost based on
      the net defined benefit asset or liability and the discount rate, measured at the beginning of the year.
      The forfeitable share incentives are allocated to employees based on vesting conditions linked to time and performance measures. The total
      shareholder return is considered in estimating the fair value of the grant at grant date. The Group allocates the number of shares per employee
      based on a formula taking into account the annual guaranteed package, percentage of gross profit and share price at grant date. The shares to
      be allocated are limited to approximately 5% of the issued share capital and vest between three and five years. The additional share scheme
      award provides for the granting of shares to eligible participating employees, equivalent in value to the increase in share price from the grant
      date (based on the specific grant price) to the vesting date.               
      Summary of material accounting policies                                     
      Post-employment benefits                                                    
      The Group provides defined benefit and defined contribution plans for the benefit of the employees. These plans are funded by the employees
      and the Group, taking into account the recommendations of the independent actuaries. The post-retirement telephone rebate liability is
      unfunded.                                                                   
      Defined benefit plans                                                       
      The Group provides defined benefit plans for pension, post-retirement medical aid benefits and telephone rebates to qualifying employees.
      The Group's net obligation in respect of defined benefits is calculated separately for each plan by estimating the amount of future benefits
      earned in return for services rendered.                                     
      The amount reported in the statement of financial position represents the present value of the defined benefit obligations, using the projected
      credit unit method, reduced by the fair value of the related plan assets. To the extent that there is uncertainty as to the entitlement to the
      surplus, no asset is recognised. The effects of this asset limitation and actuarial gains and losses are recognised in other comprehensive
      income. Interest, service cost, settlement gains or losses and curtailment gains or losses related to the defined benefit plan are recognised in
      the statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income.             
      Defined contribution plan                                                   
      Following a rule amendment on 1 July 2024, the Telkom Retirement Fund is now classified as a defined contribution plan, replacing its previous
      defined benefit status. Telkom no longer has any further obligations under IAS 19. Contributions made by Telkom are recognised as employee
      expenses. Refer to note 3.4.3 for details regarding contributions.

### [SECTION READING RESPONSE / DETERMINATION]
### 1. Answers to Stored Questions for This Section

No stored questions from earlier sections are answerable from this section's evidence. The stored ledger is dominated by dividend, treasury-share, tax, lease, hedge, and FX-repatriation questions; this section covers IAS 19 employee benefits only. The one tangential item — **Q-EQ2/Q-DIV8 (share-scheme vesting/expense timing)** — is only partially informed: the section confirms forfeitable share incentives vest over **3–5 years** and are capped at **~5% of issued share capital**, but gives no expense quantum or vesting schedule. That remains open.

### 2. Analysis of This Section (Footnotes, Accounting Policy & Disclosures)

**Key policy facts extracted:**
- **Telkom Retirement Fund reclassified from defined benefit to defined contribution effective 1 July 2024** following a rule amendment. Telkom states it "no longer has any further obligations under IAS 19" and contributions are expensed. This is a material structural change: it removes DB pension volatility from OCI/balance sheet going forward and shifts cost to a predictable cash contribution line (cross-ref **note 3.4.3**, not in evidence).
- **Discount rate methodology**: based on long-term SA Government bonds (longest JSE maturity), expected to track inflation. This is a ZAR-denominated, sovereign-linked assumption — sensitive to SA yield curve and inflation.
- **Net interest cost** measured on net DB asset/liability at beginning-of-year discount rate.
- **Asset ceiling**: no asset recognised where surplus entitlement is uncertain; actuarial gains/losses and asset-limit effects go to OCI.
- **Post-retirement telephone rebate liability is unfunded** — a pure liability with no plan assets; a legacy cost line that will run off but carries no funding offset.
- **Forfeitable share incentives**: TSR-linked, formula-based allocation (guaranteed package × % gross profit × share price at grant), vesting 3–5 years, capped ~5% of issued share capital. The "additional share scheme award" pays the *increase* in share price from grant to vest — i.e., an equity-settled appreciation instrument with mark-to-market sensitivity.

**Numbers captured (Group / Company, Rm):**

| Item | Group 2026 | Group 2025 | Company 2026 | Company 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Employee benefits — non-current assets | 1,017 | 993 | 1,017 | 993 |
| Telkom Pension Fund asset | — | 13 | — | 13 |
| Post-retirement medical aid — net plan asset recognised | 1 017 | 980 | 1 017 | 980 |

**Arithmetic / reconciliation checks:**
- Group non-current employee benefit assets: 1,017 − 13 = **1,004 ≠ 1,017**; and 993 − 13 = **980** (2025 ties). The 2026 column does **not** reconcile: the components (nil pension asset + 1,017 medical aid asset) sum to 1,017, but the total line is also 1,017 while the prior-year comparative implies the pension asset (13) was a *component* of the 993 total. Either the 2026 pension asset line is mislabelled/zeroed or the 2025 comparative includes the 13 within the 993. **Flag as verification question.**
- Medical aid net plan asset rose 980 → 1,017 (+R37m, +3.8%) — a **net asset** on a post-retirement medical scheme is unusual and implies plan assets exceed the DBO (surplus), recognised only to the extent entitlement is not uncertain. Needs confirmation of the gross DBO vs fair value of plan assets and the asset-ceiling test.
- Company = Group for all lines (no subsidiary-level DB exposure disclosed here).

**Forecast implications:** DB pension de-risking (DC conversion) is a positive for earnings predictability and removes OCI noise; the residual exposures are (i) post-retirement medical aid surplus/asset-ceiling sensitivity, (ii) unfunded telephone rebate liability, and (iii) share-based payment expense (equity-settled, non-cash, but dilutive and TSR-sensitive).

### 2. Unpacking Footnotes and Qualifications

**Footnote [^1] (p.110):** "The net actuarial gain on the TRF is up until 1 July 2024, the date of the settlement of the TRF in the prior year." — This confirms the Telkom Retirement Fund (TRF) was **settled/curtailed on 1 July 2024** and reclassified to a defined contribution plan. The R154m actuarial gain shown in the 2025 comparative column is a **one-off, non-recurring item** that will not repeat. For forecasting, the TRF line should be treated as **zero from FY2026 onward** — no DB obligation, no actuarial volatility, no net finance cost. The only ongoing cost is the employer contribution (referenced to note 3.4.2/3.4.3, not yet read).

**Discount rate compression (p.110):** Every discount rate fell year-on-year — Pension Fund 9.20%→8.50%, Medical aid 10.20%→9.20%, Telephone rebate 10.80%→9.50%, Long service 9.10%→8.80%. This is a **material assumption change** that inflates the DB obligation (lower discount rate = higher PV of liabilities) and drives the actuarial losses. The medical aid net actuarial loss of R57m (2026) vs R103m (2025) is partly offset by the lower loss, but the direction of travel on rates is the key forecast risk: if rates fall further, the R1,017m net plan asset could reverse.

**Pension increase allowance collapse (p.110):** 6.30%→2.40% — a **390bp cut**. This is the single largest assumption swing in the table and directly reduces the Pension Fund obligation. Combined with the discount rate cut, the net effect on the Pension Fund asset (R13m→R0) is that the fund has been **fully run down / settled**. The Pension Fund asset is now nil — no further DB pension asset to forecast.

**Medical aid net plan asset R1,017m (2026) vs R980m (2025):** The asset **grew R37m** despite a R57m actuarial loss. This implies **employer contributions + expected return on assets exceeded** the actuarial loss + benefit payments. The reconciliation is not shown in this section — this is a **verification gap** (see Q-EB1 below). The asset is a **non-current asset** on the balance sheet; it is not cash and cannot be used for liquidity forecasting. It is a **surplus recognition** subject to IAS 19 asset ceiling — the note says "to the extent there is uncertainty as to entitlement to surplus, no asset is recognised," yet R1,017m IS recognised, implying management judges the surplus recoverable (via contribution holidays or refund). This is a **judgemental asset** — flag for impairment risk.

**Telephone rebate unfunded (p.109):** Explicitly stated as unfunded. This is a **DB obligation with no plan assets** — pure liability. Duration 8.0 years (longest of all plans). The R20m actuarial gain in 2026 (vs R44m loss in 2025) is assumption-driven, not cash. For forecasting, treat as a **long-dated unfunded liability** with cash cost = benefit payments only.

**Share incentives (p.109):** "Limited to approximately 5% of issued share capital" and "vest between three and five years." The TSR-linked and "additional share scheme award" (share price increase from grant to vest) are **equity-settled** — non-cash, but dilutive. The 5% cap is a **potential dilution ceiling** — material for per-share forecasts. Expense quantum not disclosed here (→ Q-EB5).

**Duration table (p.110):** Pension Fund duration fell 4.3→3.7 years (fund winding down). Medical aid 6.5→6.6, telephone rebate 7.9→8.0, long service 4.1→4.4 — all **lengthening slightly**, meaning liabilities are getting **more long-dated**, increasing interest-rate sensitivity. Next full valuation 31 March 2027 — **no re-measurement until FY2027**, so FY2026 assumptions carry into FY2027 interim.

**Mortality:** Longevities increased (males 17.00→17.10, females 21.30→21.50) — **liabilities increase** with longevity, a slow adverse drift.
